name: 218th Judicial District Court of Texas
region: Atascosa, Frio, Karnes, La Salle and Wilson Counties, Texas, USA
description: Zoom court dockets of the 218th Judicial District Court of Texas, a rural trial court covering Atascosa, Frio, Karnes, La Salle and Wilson counties, recorded between October 2020 and early 2022. The district judge hears criminal, civil and family cases with prosecutors, defense counsel, defendants, probation officers, parties and interpreters. The court takes pleas, imposes sentences and probation conditions, rules on probation revocations and bond, grants civil judgments, issues family-law orders, and sets cases for later hearings and jury trials.
sensitivity: Includes custody, protective-order and other family-law hearings about children.
Criminal defendants are named; dates of birth are sometimes stated.
meetings_about: Eighty-eight Zoom dockets from October 2020 to early 2022, held county by county and averaging almost 4 hours; the longest run 7 to 8 hours. The judge calls a criminal, civil or family docket case by case, taking announcements from attorneys, marking no-shows, and setting or resetting dates, with the court administrator posting dates in chat. Pleas, revocation and adjudication hearings, and contested evidentiary hearings are held on the record. Breakout rooms are used for attorney-client conferences, including with defendants appearing from county jails. There are also special settings for single cases and a few joint Karnes/Wilson (and Atascosa) juvenile board meetings.
participants: The district judge (occasionally a different judge on a special setting); the court coordinator and court administrator; district clerks and court reporters; assistant district attorneys; defense counsel; defendants, some appearing from jail; community supervision (probation) officers; interpreters; attorneys and parties in civil and family cases; witnesses; juvenile probation staff and county officials at juvenile board meetings.
decisions: Criminal: plea admonishments and acceptance of plea bargains and open pleas, adjudication of guilt, sentences and probation conditions, motions to revoke or adjudicate probation, bond matters, competency and pretrial diversion matters, and settings for docket call and jury selection. Civil: default and summary judgments, including tax suits and property cases. Family: divorce, custody, child support and termination-of-parental-rights matters, and protective orders. Juvenile board meetings approve juvenile probation budgets and administrative matters.
notes: Includes family-law hearings about children (custody, support, termination of parental rights) and protective orders. Criminal defendants are named and dates of birth are sometimes stated. Some hearings use Spanish interpretation, but ASR ran in English only. The 81st and 218th District Courts share these counties, and some cases and staff are identified with the 81st. A court coordinator's shared tile and jail tiles carry some turns. Some recordings begin with pre-hearing chatter.

name: Hidalgo County Court at Law No. 9
type: County court at law (civil, family and misdemeanor criminal)
description: Recordings of Zoom dockets of Hidalgo County Court at Law No. 9 in Texas, covering civil, family and misdemeanor criminal matters. Participants are the judge, court staff, prosecutors, defense and civil attorneys, parties and defendants (some self-represented), probation officers and Spanish-language interpreters. The court grants divorces and sets custody and child support, issues protective orders, rules on civil judgments and dismissals, and in criminal cases accepts pleas, imposes sentences and probation, and rules on bond and probation-revocation matters.
sensitivity: Defendants state personal phone numbers on the record, hundreds of times across the collection.
Criminal defendants are named.
meetings_about: Zoom dockets of a county court at law, mostly titled as the judge's personal Zoom room and otherwise as morning/afternoon civil or criminal dockets and a dismissal-for-want-of-prosecution (DWOP) docket. Civil sessions cover family-law matters (divorce prove-ups, custody and conservatorship, child support, protective orders) and general civil matters (default judgments, summary-judgment motions, status hearings). Criminal sessions are misdemeanor dockets with plea announcements, pleas, motions to revoke probation and bond/driving-license matters. The court goes live and on the record at the start; attorneys announce cases by docket number. Sessions run from about 25 minutes to over 3 hours. On occasion the judge covers the criminal docket of County Court at Law No. 8.
participants: The presiding judge; the court coordinator, clerk and bailiff; assistant district attorneys; defense attorneys and family-law/civil attorneys; defendants, parties and witnesses (some self-represented); adult probation officers; and Spanish-language interpreters.
decisions: In family and civil cases the court grants divorces and approves agreed decrees, sets conservatorship, possession and child support, issues protective orders, grants default and summary judgments, dismisses cases for want of prosecution and sets hearings. In criminal cases it accepts guilty/no-contest pleas, imposes sentences, fines and probation terms, rules on motions to revoke, sets bond conditions and grants occupational driver's licenses (e.g. with ignition interlock).
notes: Frequent Spanish interpretation; ASR ran in English, so interpreted Spanish is poorly transcribed. Criminal defendants and family-law parties are named, personal phone numbers are stated hundreds of times, and family hearings discuss children, custody, protective orders and mental health. Almost all recording dates in metadata are a single upload date (2022-09-21), not hearing dates; spoken dates show hearings from 2021. A few sessions are the County Court at Law No. 8 docket handled by this judge. The judge's display name varies across many tile spellings.

name: Bexar County Court at Law No. 6
description: Recordings of Zoom criminal dockets of Bexar County Court at Law No. 6 in San Antonio, Texas, from 2021 and 2022, including arraignment, pretrial, plea and probation-revocation hearings, many held as the Bexar County Veterans Treatment Court. Participants are the judge, court staff, assistant district attorneys, defense attorneys, defendants and probation officers, with occasional Spanish interpretation. The judge accepts pleas and plea agreements, places defendants on probation or pretrial diversion, rules on motions to revoke community supervision, and imposes sentences and supervision conditions in misdemeanor cases.
sensitivity: Criminal defendants are named on screen and in speech.
Phone numbers are read aloud, mostly the probation office's but some personal.
meetings_about: Zoom criminal dockets of a statutory county court, 2021-2022, titled as arraignment, pretrial conference, plea, motion-to-revoke (MTR) and VTC dockets. The court also sits as the Bexar County Veterans Treatment Court, and many sessions take up Veterans Treatment Court pretrial-diversion pleas and probation agreements. The judge opens by announcing the court, date and the cause numbers and attorneys set for the day, then takes cases one at a time, including sworn testimony from probation officers in revocation hearings. Sessions usually run 20 to 110 minutes.
participants: The presiding judge; the court coordinator/clerk; assistant criminal district attorneys for the State; defense attorneys (retained and appointed); defendants; community supervision (CSCD/probation) officers who are sworn to testify; and occasionally family members and Spanish-language interpreters.
decisions: The judge arraigns defendants and sets cases, accepts guilty/no-contest pleas and plea agreements, places defendants on community supervision or deferred adjudication, admits veterans to Veterans Treatment Court pretrial diversion, rules on motions to revoke probation or adjudicate guilt (pleas of true/not true), imposes sentences (jail time, fines, court costs), modifies supervision conditions and handles bond matters.
notes: Criminal defendants are named on screen and in speech; case numbers and some personal phone numbers are read aloud. Spanish interpretation occurs in about a third of recordings and the English-only ASR transcribes it poorly. The channel names no jurisdiction; Bexar County is established by the judge's spoken openings. Some cases involve veterans' mental health and substance treatment.

name: Township of Montague Council and committees
description: Zoom recordings of the council and committees of the Township of Montague, a rural township in Lanark County, Ontario, from 2020 to 2022. Most are combined Council and Committee of the Whole meetings led by the Reeve with the Deputy Reeve, councillors and township staff, alongside special budget meetings, Recreation and Culture Committee meetings and Committee of Adjustment hearings. Council passes by-laws, adopts budgets and acts on staff reports, and the Committee of Adjustment decides minor variance applications.
sensitivity: Street addresses are read out.
meetings_about: Mostly combined regular Council and Committee of the Whole meetings (typically 2-4 hours, evenings, live-streamed to YouTube), plus special meetings of council and of the Committee of the Whole (including budget workshops), Recreation and Culture Committee meetings (about 25-90 min) and Committee of Adjustment hearings (15-20 min). Council meetings open with a moment of silence, adoption of the agenda and minutes, disclosure of interest, delegations, staff reports, by-laws, correspondence and closed sessions; motions are read with mover and seconder and carried by voice.
participants: The Reeve (presiding), Deputy Reeve and councillors; township staff including the clerk-administrator, treasurer, public works manager, fire chief, planner and deputy clerk; consulting engineers and other delegations; committee members of the Recreation and Culture Committee; applicants and neighbours at Committee of Adjustment hearings.
decisions: Council passes by-laws (including zoning by-law amendments), adopts the annual budget after workshops, receives and approves staff reports and recommendations (roads, equipment purchases, agreements with Lanark County), and approves Committee of the Whole minutes and recommendations. The Committee of Adjustment grants or refuses minor variances under the Ontario Planning Act, often as conditions of land severances. The Recreation Committee plans community events and programs.
notes: Many tiles carry first names or device names rather than identifiable officials; a township host tile carries some turns. Street addresses and property owners are named in planning items. Many early recordings share one upload date (2020-12-22) that is not the meeting date.

name: Austin County Court at Law
description: Zoom recordings of the Austin County Court at Law in Texas, consisting of the judge's morning and afternoon dockets and individually scheduled hearings and trials. Participants include the presiding judge, court reporter, prosecutors, defense and family-law attorneys, attorneys ad litem, parties, witnesses and occasional interpreters. The court handles misdemeanor criminal cases, family law including divorce, custody and CPS matters, probate and heirship proceedings, and civil disputes. Decisions made on the record include accepting pleas and imposing sentences or probation, setting bonds and continuances, and issuing custody, property and probate orders.
sensitivity: Titles and speech name criminal defendants; phone numbers are sometimes read aloud.
meetings_about: Zoom court sessions of a single county court at law judge, posted as morning and afternoon 'CCL Zoom docket' recordings (some labeled pretrial, CPS, or P&A) plus individually titled hearings and trials identified by cause number. Sessions run from about 15 minutes to several hours; the judge calls each cause number, has participants announce appearances, swears witnesses, and hears testimony and argument. The docket mixes criminal misdemeanor matters, family law (divorce, custody/visitation, CPS cases), probate/heirship, small civil disputes, and at least one multi-day civil trial by the State of Texas.
participants: The presiding judge, a court reporter/court staff, prosecutors and defense attorneys, family-law and civil attorneys, attorneys ad litem and amicus/appointed counsel, defendants, parties to civil and family cases, witnesses, and occasional interpreters.
decisions: The judge accepts plea agreements and pronounces sentences in misdemeanor cases (e.g. DWI, possession of marijuana, resisting arrest: jail with credit for time served, fines and costs, probation/community supervision, deferred findings), sets bond and continuance matters, issues family-law orders on conservatorship, visitation and property division, rules in CPS/parental-rights and name-change matters, and determines heirship and related probate matters.
notes: Titles and speech name criminal defendants, family-law litigants and heirs; family and CPS hearings discuss children and parental-rights termination; phone numbers are sometimes read aloud. Some sessions use Spanish interpretation. About a quarter of transcribed meetings were excluded for lack of a usable gallery view (document screen-shares). Recordings often begin before the judge goes on the record, with off-record chatter.

name: Temple Municipal Court
description: Recordings of Zoom court-appearance sessions of the Temple Municipal Court in Texas, which hears Class C misdemeanor and city cases, mostly traffic citations, from 2020 to 2022. Participants are the municipal judge, court clerks, the city prosecutor, and defendants, including teenagers appearing with parents. The judge explains plea options, accepts pleas, and sets fines, payment plans, community service, deferred dispositions, driving safety courses and teen court referrals, and schedules pretrial or trial settings for contested cases.
sensitivity: Defendants are named; dates of birth and phone numbers are stated.
meetings_about: Zoom court-appearance sessions for defendants cited for Class C misdemeanors (traffic offenses such as speeding, driving without insurance or with an invalid license, school-zone and parking violations, and other city cases). The judge opens each session with an extended explanation of the three pleas (guilty, not guilty, no contest) and of the ways to resolve a case (teen court, deferred disposition, driving safety course, payment plans, community service). Defendants are then taken one by one; those pleading not guilty are moved to a separate online pretrial meeting with the city prosecutor and return afterward. Sessions run about 35 minutes to 3 hours.
participants: The municipal judge; court clerks; the city prosecutor; defendants (including teenagers appearing with a parent) and occasionally defense attorneys.
decisions: The judge accepts pleas, sets fines and court costs, grants payment plans or orders community service in place of payment (based on income), grants deferred disposition, driving safety course dismissals and teen court referrals, waives fines on indigence, recalls or clears warrants and license holds, and sets pretrial and bench-trial dates for contested cases.
notes: Defendants are named, and dates of birth, phone numbers and financial circumstances are stated. Minors (teen court candidates) and their parents appear. The judge's display tile varies across many misspelled variants, and a clerk-of-court tile carries some turns. Most metadata dates are a single upload date (2022-09-07), not hearing dates.

name: City of Lakewood City Council and advisory boards/commissions
description: Zoom recordings of public meetings of the City of Lakewood, Washington, mostly City Council regular meetings and study sessions, plus meetings of city advisory boards and commissions such as the Arts Commission, Planning Commission, Public Safety Advisory Committee and Parks and Recreation Advisory Board. Participants include the mayor and councilmembers, the city manager, clerk and department staff, board and commission members, and members of the public. The council adopts ordinances, resolutions and budgets, approves consent agendas and contracts, and holds public hearings, while the advisory bodies review programs and make recommendations to the council.
sensitivity: Phone numbers and street addresses are occasionally read out.
meetings_about: Virtual meetings from April 2020 to December 2022. Most (about 47 of 74) are Lakewood City Council meetings, including regular business meetings, Monday study sessions and two special meetings, typically 1-3.5 hours (average about 2 hours 10 minutes). The rest are advisory and citizen bodies: Arts Commission and its Public Art Subcommittee, Public Safety Advisory Committee, Planning Commission, Parks and Recreation Advisory Board, Civil Service Commission, Lakewood's Promise Advisory Board, and a joint council/Clover Park School District board meeting. Council meetings follow a standard agenda: call to order and roll call by the clerk, public comment, consent agenda, ordinances and resolutions, public hearings, unfinished and new business, and staff briefings; advisory boards approve minutes and hear staff and member reports.
participants: The mayor (presiding) and city councilmembers, the city manager, city clerk and department staff (police chief, parks, planning, finance), advisory board and commission chairs and members, staff liaisons, fire district representatives, and members of the public giving comment or testimony at hearings.
decisions: The City Council adopts ordinances (including the biennial budget and budget amendments), resolutions and numbered motions, approves the consent agenda, contracts and appointments, and holds public hearings on land use, zoning and comprehensive plan matters; study sessions are discussion only. Advisory boards approve minutes and make recommendations (e.g. public art projects such as utility box wraps, park capital projects, public safety outreach) rather than binding decisions.
notes: Phone numbers and street addresses are occasionally read out. Some Zoom tiles carry first names only or room names (e.g. 'American Lake'), so attribution for some speakers is unresolved; about 6% of words have no speaker name. Advisory board recordings often include informal pre-meeting chatter. One council recording is marked partial.

name: City of Sault Ste. Marie City Council and committees/boards
description: Zoom recordings of public meetings of the City of Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, consisting mainly of City Council regular, special and budget meetings, plus committees and boards such as the Committee of Adjustment, Environmental Sustainability Committee, Historic Sites Board, Municipal Heritage Committee, Cultural Vitality Committee and Tourism Sault Ste. Marie. Participants include the mayor and councillors, the city clerk and staff, committee members, delegations, and applicants and residents at hearings. Council passes by-laws, sets the budget and tax levy, and decides rezoning and official plan matters, while the Committee of Adjustment rules on minor variances and consents and the advisory bodies make recommendations.
sensitivity: Street addresses are frequently read out.
meetings_about: Virtual meetings from May 2020 to November 2022. About half (36 of 75) are City Council meetings: regular meetings roughly every two weeks (typically 2-3.5 hours), special meetings (e.g. on the new official plan), and multi-hour budget meetings. The rest are committees and boards: Committee of Adjustment hearings, Environmental Sustainability Committee, Historic Sites Board, Municipal Heritage Committee, Cultural Vitality Committee and cultural policy sub-committee meetings, Tourism Sault Ste. Marie board meetings, the Economic Development Corporation board and AGM, and an Accessibility Advisory Committee. Council meetings open with a land acknowledgement (Robinson-Huron Treaty territory, Garden River and Batchewana First Nations), adoption of the agenda and declarations of pecuniary interest, then delegations, a consent agenda, staff reports, by-laws and recorded votes, run by the mayor with the city clerk reading motions.
participants: The mayor (or acting mayor) and city councillors, the city clerk and deputy clerk, the CAO and city staff (planning, finance, public works, legal, environmental), committee and board chairs and citizen members, delegations, development applicants and agents, and neighbouring residents at Committee of Adjustment hearings.
decisions: Council passes by-laws (including zoning by-law amendments and the official plan), approves the annual budget and tax levy, rezoning applications, staff recommendations on the consent agenda and council resolutions, with declared conflicts of interest recorded. The Committee of Adjustment grants or refuses minor variances and consents (land severances). Advisory committees and boards approve minutes, review programs (e.g. climate/retrofit initiatives, heritage designation, cultural grants and policy, municipal election accessibility, tourism budgets) and make recommendations.
notes: Street addresses of properties and applicants are frequently read out, especially at Committee of Adjustment hearings. About 6% of words have no speaker name; Zoom tiles use role-prefixed names (e.g. 'Councillor <surname>') with OCR noise. Some committee recordings begin mid-conversation.

name: Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal
region: Florida, USA (court seated in Daytona Beach)
description: Zoom recordings of oral arguments before three-judge panels of Florida's Fifth District Court of Appeal, one appellate case per recording. Appellate attorneys for each side, including assistant attorneys general in criminal appeals, present timed arguments and answer questions from the judges. The cases span civil and criminal appeals from trial courts; the panel takes each case under advisement and no decision is announced during the recording.
sensitivity: Arguments name private litigants.
meetings_about: Zoom oral arguments, one case per recording (titles give the appellate case number), typically 25-60 minutes. The presiding judge opens the session, introduces the three-judge panel (sometimes including an associate judge sitting by designation), names the case, notes that each side has about 20 minutes and that the appellant may reserve time (usually five minutes) for rebuttal, and states that arguments are live-streamed. Appellant's counsel argues, the appellee responds, the appellant gives rebuttal, with frequent questions from the bench; the panel then takes the case under advisement and adjourns.
participants: Panels of three appellate judges (including the chief judge), appellate counsel for appellants and appellees in civil cases (e.g. insurance, foreclosure, employment, contract, municipal matters), and in criminal appeals defense counsel and assistant attorneys general for the State. Parties themselves do not usually speak.
decisions: No rulings are announced at argument; panels hear argument and take cases under advisement, with written decisions issued later (not part of the recordings). Arguments concern whether trial-court judgments, jury instructions, suppression rulings and summary judgments should be affirmed or reversed.
notes: Recording dates in the metadata are mostly a single upload date (2022-10-12), not the argument date. Case captions and arguments name private litigants and discuss criminal facts. The channel's earliest in-person courtroom videos and one meeting without participant names are excluded.

name: Ohio First District Court of Appeals
description: Zoom recordings of oral arguments before three-judge panels of the Ohio First District Court of Appeals, which hears appeals from Hamilton County, dated 2020-2022. Counsel for appellants and appellees, including state and city prosecutors, defense attorneys, private counsel and occasional self-represented litigants, argue criminal, civil, juvenile and family appeals while the judges question them. Decisions are not announced at argument: each case is taken under submission for a later written opinion.
sensitivity: Arguments discuss child-abuse, juvenile-delinquency and guardianship matters.
meetings_about: Zoom oral arguments before three-judge panels, 2020-2022, usually one to several cases per recording (about 20-105 minutes). A presiding judge welcomes parties to the First District Court of Appeals, calls the case number and caption, asks appellant's counsel to reserve rebuttal time, and the panel questions counsel throughout; each argument ends with the case taken under submission. Cases cover criminal appeals, civil disputes (e.g. summary judgment, property valuation, tort immunity) and juvenile, custody and protective-order matters.
participants: Panels of appellate judges (one presiding); appellant and appellee counsel, including prosecutors for the State or City of Cincinnati, public defenders and appointed or private counsel, and occasionally pro se litigants.
decisions: No rulings are announced at argument. The presiding judge takes each case under submission and says the court will issue a timely written opinion or decision later.
notes: Arguments discuss criminal facts, child custody, juvenile and protective-order matters, and name parties via case captions. Many recordings span several cases; titles often give only the argument date.

name: City of Norman City Council
description: Zoom meetings of the Norman City Council in Norman, Oklahoma, recorded between April 2020 and May 2021, including conference and regular meetings, study sessions, special sessions and council committees. The mayor, council members, the city clerk, city manager, city attorney and department staff take part, and many residents give public comment. The council votes on ordinances such as rezonings and a COVID-19 mask ordinance, the annual budget including police funding, contracts, bond elections and appointments.
meetings_about: Thirty-two Zoom meetings from April 2020 to May 2021 (many uploaded in 2022). They include combined council conference and regular meetings, study sessions, special sessions (including a swearing-in session), and the Council Oversight Committee and Community Planning and Transportation Committee. Regular meetings are also convened as the Norman Utilities Authority, Norman Municipal Authority and Norman Tax Increment Finance Authority. They are long, often 4 to 7.5 hours. A conference session with staff presentations comes first. The regular meeting follows with a clerk's roll call, the Pledge of Allegiance, numbered agenda items, motion and second, council discussion, public comment on items, and roll-call votes. Committee meetings are 1 to 2 hours of staff reports and discussion.
participants: The mayor, council members representing wards, the city clerk calling roll, the city manager, the city attorney, department staff (utilities, planning, transit, finance, police), applicants' attorneys on zoning items, and many members of the public commenting by Zoom, phone or written comments read into the record.
decisions: Ordinances, including rezonings on first and final reading and COVID-19 measures such as a mask ordinance; adoption of the annual budget, including a contested police budget; contracts and change orders (e.g. water-line replacement); calling a general obligation bond election; appointing a council member to fill a ward vacancy; approval of minutes and consent items. Study sessions and committees discuss items and give staff direction without final action.
notes: Only meetings verified as gallery view are included; the channel often used a screen-share layout. Meetings are very long, with extended public comment on contentious topics (mask ordinance, police budget). A generic 'Public' tile carries some comments. Many upload dates (2022-09-15) differ from the actual meeting dates in the titles.

name: Waipā District Council
type: District council, committees and community boards
description: Livestreamed Zoom and hybrid recordings of Waipā District Council in the Waikato region of New Zealand, covering full council, standing committees such as Finance and Corporate, Strategic Planning and Policy, Audit and Risk, Regulatory and Service Delivery, the Cambridge and Te Awamutu community boards, the Pirongia Ward Committee, the Iwi Consultative Committee, workshops and hearings. Participants include the mayor, councillors, community board and committee members, iwi representatives, council staff, submitters, applicants and members of the public. The bodies adopt policies, plans, bylaws and financial reports, hear submissions, decide resource consent applications, and allocate community grants.
sensitivity: Iwi Consultative Committee recordings involve Māori representatives; Māori data sovereignty considerations apply.
meetings_about: 71 livestreamed meetings (6 minutes to about 4.5 hours) held on Zoom or in hybrid form during and after COVID-19 lockdowns; recordings carry no titles or dates, but the proceedings refer to 2020-2023. They cover full council meetings, standing committees (Finance and Corporate, Strategic Planning and Policy, Audit and Risk, Service Delivery, Regulatory, District Promotion), the Cambridge and Te Awamutu community boards, the Pirongia Ward Committee, the Iwi Consultative Committee, staff-led council workshops (e.g. transport strategy, resource management reform), hearings of public submissions (e.g. on the representation review and annual/long-term plans, with timed ten-minute presentations), and Regulatory Committee hearings on resource consent applications. Meetings typically open with a karakia or mihi in te reo Māori, apologies, disclosure of members' interests and confirmation of the order of business, then work through staff reports, public forum and resolutions voted by 'all in favour, aye', with public-excluded items taken separately.
participants: The mayor ('Your Worship') and councillors, committee chairs and independent/external members (e.g. on Audit and Risk), community board chairs and members, iwi and Māori representatives on the Iwi Consultative Committee, the chief executive, group managers and council staff (finance, planning, service delivery, emergency management), auditors, consultants and applicants' experts at hearings, submitters, and members of the public speaking in public forum.
decisions: Council and committees adopt reports, policies, bylaws and financial reports, and consider annual plan, long-term plan and representation review submissions; the Audit and Risk Committee reviews audit and risk reporting; the Regulatory Committee hears and decides resource consent applications and objections; community boards allocate discretionary fund grants to local groups and make recommendations to council; the Iwi Consultative Committee and workshops provide advice and discussion rather than binding decisions.
notes: Meeting titles and dates are missing from the metadata; body and date are established only from the recordings. Te reo Māori is spoken (karakia, mihi, Iwi Consultative Committee business) and was transcribed by English ASR, so it is poorly rendered; Māori data sovereignty considerations apply to Iwi Consultative Committee recordings. Some meetings are hybrid with in-chamber participants on a shared council host tile (about 6% of attributed words). Hearings name private applicants, submitters and neighbouring residents with street addresses.

name: El Paso County Justice of the Peace Court, Precinct 1
description: Zoom recordings of hearings in the Justice of the Peace Court, Precinct 1, in El Paso County, Texas, from 2020 to 2022, mostly titled by case number. The justice of the peace hears eviction, debt-claim and small-claims cases, Class C misdemeanor and truancy cases, driver's-license and show-cause dockets. Participants include landlords, tenants, attorneys, legal-aid lawyers, school attendance officers, a state driver-license representative and Spanish interpreters, and the judge rules from the bench on evictions, judgments, fines and license matters.
sensitivity: Individual cases are identified by case number in titles; defendants and eviction parties are named.
meetings_about: Zoom hearings of a Texas justice court, mostly one case per recording titled by case number: eviction trials (-FED, about half), civil and small-claims/debt-claim cases (-CV, -DB, including motions for summary disposition), criminal Class C and truancy cases (-CR, -TRU), plus grouped dockets titled DL Hearings, Administrative Hearings, Show-Cause Hearings, DWOP (dismissal for want of prosecution) Hearings and Traffic Court. Hearings typically run 15-50 minutes (a traffic docket 130 minutes); the judge swears in parties, takes testimony and rules from the bench.
participants: The justice of the peace presiding, court staff, landlords, property managers and their attorneys or filing agents, tenants and their legal-aid attorneys, creditor attorneys, defendants in traffic and Class C cases and their counsel, school-district attendance officers and parents in truancy cases, a Texas DPS representative in driver's-license hearings, and Spanish interpreters.
decisions: Grants or denies evictions and sets writ-of-possession dates and appeal bond amounts; decides debt and small-claims cases; enters findings and fines, payment plans, deferral/driving-safety conditions, extensions or warrants in show-cause and traffic matters; decides truancy cases; rules on driver's-license suspension and occupational-license matters; dismisses cases for want of prosecution.
notes: Parties (tenants, defendants, parents) are named; truancy cases involve minors and school records; some hearings are in Spanish or interpreted. The judge's courtroom tile appears in every meeting and often carries voices of other people in the room, so speaker attribution is noisy; device-named tiles carry some words. Over a third of transcribed meetings lacked a usable gallery view. Most recording dates are an upload date (2022-06-03), not the hearing date.

name: Town of Lewisboro Town Board and Planning Board
description: Zoom recordings from the Town of Lewisboro, New York, dated 2020-2022, most of them Planning Board meetings, with some Town Board, police reform and comprehensive plan committee meetings. Board members, town consultants and counsel review development applications presented by applicants and their attorneys and engineers, and residents speak at public hearings and public comment periods. The Planning Board votes on environmental determinations and site plan, subdivision, wetland and special permit resolutions, while the Town Board adopts the budget, awards bids and passes resolutions.
sensitivity: Street addresses are frequently read out.
meetings_about: Mostly monthly Planning Board meetings (about 20 of 28 recordings, often 90-225 minutes, many including public hearings), plus Town Board meetings, a Police Reform and Reinvention meeting, and Comprehensive Plan steering committee meetings, 2020-2022. Planning Board meetings open with the chair's statement on the Open Meetings Law and videoconferencing, roll of members and consultants, then take applications in turn, with public comment only during noticed public hearings. Town Board meetings, chaired by the town supervisor, include public comment periods (two minutes, residents/property owners), public hearings, budget presentations and resolutions.
participants: Planning Board chair and members, the board's planning/wetland consultant, counsel and administrator; applicants with their attorneys and engineers; Town Supervisor and Town Board members, town attorney, town clerk and department heads (e.g. facilities, police); residents who comment at hearings.
decisions: The Planning Board adopts SEQRA negative declarations and resolutions granting or extending site plan, subdivision/lot-line, wetland and special use permits, releases performance bonds, and opens, continues or closes public hearings. The Town Board adopts the town budget, awards bids, votes on resolutions and agreements, and responds to proposals such as a group-home siting under New York's Padavan Law; committees develop recommendations on police reform and the comprehensive plan.
notes: Dominated by Planning Board land-use proceedings. Property addresses and applicant names are read out frequently. Some meetings are long (up to about 4 hours).

name: City of Beaumont Council
description: Recordings of City of Beaumont (Alberta) council meetings held on Zoom from 2020 to 2022, including regular and special council meetings and Committee of the Whole. The mayor chairs, councillors debate and vote, city administration presents reports, and residents occasionally speak at the open forum or at public hearings. Council passes bylaws such as land use amendments and a COVID-19 face-covering bylaw, approves budget amendments, capital projects and council policies, and gives direction to administration.
meetings_about: 26 meetings from April 2020 to March 2022, mostly regular council meetings, plus special council meetings and Committee of the Whole meetings. Most run 1.5-3.5 hours. The mayor calls the meeting to order and gives a Treaty 6 land acknowledgement, sometimes followed by proclamations. Next come agenda changes from administration, a consent agenda (minutes and information items), an open forum for registered members of the public, public hearings on bylaws, presentations and delegations, and business items. Closed sessions are moved into but not broadcast. Members ask to speak with Zoom's raise-hand function, and votes are by show of hands ('all in favour').
participants: The mayor (chair of council), six councillors (one of whom chairs Committee of the Whole), the chief administrative officer and legislative staff, city directors and planners (finance, recreation, planning, communications), outside presenters such as the local provincial MLA and community groups, and residents speaking at the open forum or public hearings.
decisions: Council passes bylaws on first, second and third reading, for example a temporary face-covering bylaw and land use bylaw amendments that redistrict neighbourhoods. It holds statutory public hearings. It approves budget and capital-plan amendments, financial reports and surplus transfers, and adopts council policies (investment, taxation, land management, public participation). It approves capital projects and debenture borrowing, acts on notices of motion, and accepts reports as information.
notes: A tile named for the city (a chamber camera) carries some turns, and those turns belong to a room, not a person (about 11% of attributed words are on shared or role tiles). Some speaker labels differ in spelling between meetings. Closed-session items are listed on the agenda but not recorded.

name: Supreme Court of Guam
description: Virtual proceedings of the Supreme Court of Guam, the territory's highest court, recorded between 2020 and 2022. They are mostly oral arguments in criminal and civil appeals, in which a three-justice panel questions counsel for the government and for appellants or appellees. The court takes each case under advisement and issues written opinions later, so rulings are not announced in the recordings. The collection also includes status and disqualification hearings, rule promulgation hearings and a bar admission ceremony.
sensitivity: Captions name private litigants; dates of birth are occasionally stated.
meetings_about: Fifty-one virtual proceedings (2020 to 2022), most of them appellate oral arguments of about 45 to 90 minutes in criminal (CRA) and civil (CVA) appeals, writ petitions and a request for a declaratory judgment (CRQ). The clerk opens court and calls the case, naming the parties, counsel and the three-justice panel. Each side argues (under the virtual procedure, first with five uninterrupted minutes), justices question counsel, and the appellant gives rebuttal. Other recordings are short status and disqualification hearings that confirm the panel and argument dates, a status conference, rule promulgation hearings, and a Guam Bar admission ceremony.
participants: The Chief Justice presiding and associate justices (sometimes justices pro tempore); the courtroom clerk; appellate counsel, including assistant attorneys general for the People of Guam, public defenders and private attorneys; counsel for government agencies; court staff presenting proposed rules; bar association officers and bar candidates at the admission ceremony.
decisions: No rulings are announced at oral argument. The panel takes each case under advisement and issues a written opinion later. Status and disqualification hearings record counsel's objections, if any, to the panel and confirm argument dates. Promulgation hearings take presentations on proposed court rules, and the admission ceremony admits new attorneys to the Guam Bar.
notes: Case captions in titles and the clerk's case calls name private litigants, including criminal defendants and parties in family and guardianship appeals. Appeals may discuss criminal facts and family matters. Many upload dates (2022-03-22) are not argument dates. One argument was held before a school audience for Law Day.

name: Chambers County Probate Court and Commissioners Court
description: Zoom recordings from Chambers County, Texas, covering both the county judge's probate dockets and meetings of the Commissioners Court, which share a channel and a presiding county judge. In probate hearings, attorneys question applicants and witnesses about decedents' estates or proposed guardianships, and the judge admits wills, declares heirship, issues letters testamentary or of administration and approves guardianships. In Commissioners Court meetings, the county judge and commissioners hear staff and outside reports and vote on resolutions, bids, road projects and other county business.
sensitivity: Probate dockets concern private estates and guardianships.
meetings_about: Two kinds of recordings from one county channel: about 46 probate dockets (typically 15-70 minutes) in which the county judge calls the court to order, swears in all witnesses at once and takes each cause number (e.g. 20CPR0094) in turn; and 14 regular and special called Commissioners Court meetings (roughly 15-190 minutes) that open with call to order, invocation and pledge, then work through numbered agenda items with motions, seconds and voice votes.
participants: Probate dockets: the county judge presiding, a court clerk who calls the docket and administers the oath, probate attorneys, applicants and witnesses (heirs, executors, proposed guardians), and occasionally attorneys ad litem. Commissioners Court: the county judge as chair, four county commissioners, county department heads and staff (e.g. road and bridge, health/emergency management), outside presenters such as auditors and state highway officials, and occasional public speakers.
decisions: Probate: the judge admits wills to probate (including as muniments of title), grants letters testamentary or of administration, signs judgments declaring heirship, sets administration bonds, approves ad litem fees and grants guardianships of incapacitated persons, usually ruling from the bench at the end of each case. Commissioners Court: votes on resolutions, acceptance of audit reports, bids and road/bridge projects, grant applications and other county business.
notes: Pools judicial probate dockets (majority of recordings) with legislative Commissioners Court meetings. Probate testimony names decedents, heirs and family members and discusses private estates; guardianship hearings discuss an adult's mental health. Many pre-session connection-check chatter segments; some device-named tiles.

name: Albemarle County School Board
description: Recordings of virtual meetings of the Albemarle County School Board in Virginia from 2020 to 2022, including regular meetings, a retreat and budget work sessions. Participants are elected board members, a student representative, the superintendent and division staff, and parents, teachers and students who speak during public comment. The board votes on the school division's budget, policies, school calendar and pandemic reopening plans, and approves consent agendas by roll-call vote.
sensitivity: School boards may seat student representatives, who may be minors; public comment can concern named children.
meetings_about: Regular school board meetings, special meetings (including a two-part board retreat in June 2020), and budget/work sessions held virtually during 2020-2022. Meetings typically open by voting by roll call to enter a closed session under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act (the closed session itself is not recorded), then reconvene, certify the closed meeting, and proceed through public comment, a consent agenda, a student-led 'spotlight on education', staff presentations and action items. Recordings run roughly 1.5 to 3.5 hours.
participants: The board chair and vice chair, board members representing magisterial districts plus an at-large member, a student representative, the superintendent and deputy/assistant superintendents, division staff (budget, human resources, legal/policy, clerk), and members of the public (parents, teachers, students) speaking during public comment.
decisions: The board adopts the school operating budget and capital funding requests, approves consent agendas and division policies (e.g. mask/face-covering policy, anti-racism policy, policy on transgender students), votes on the school calendar and pandemic return-to-school plans, directs reviews such as the renaming of schools named after individuals, and certifies closed sessions by roll-call vote.
notes: The dataset directory slug is misspelled 'Albermale'. A student representative (possibly a minor) sits with the board, and public comment can concern named children. Closed sessions are voted on but not recorded. 13 of 32 transcribed meetings were excluded for lack of a usable gallery view; no released meeting keeps the active-speaker highlight above 90% of frames, and some turns are attributed to 'Unknown'.

name: Eighth Court of Appeals of Texas
description: Recordings of Zoom proceedings of the Eighth Court of Appeals of Texas, the intermediate appellate court in El Paso, from 2020 to 2022. Most are oral arguments in which a three-justice panel questions appellate counsel in civil, criminal and original-proceeding matters. A few are swearing-in ceremonies for new attorneys, a show-cause contempt hearing, and a judicial-conduct hearing before the justices sitting as a court of review. Cases are taken under advisement and decided later in written opinions, which are not part of the recordings.
sensitivity: Arguments name private litigants.
meetings_about: 38 recordings dated 2020-2022, most about 50-70 minutes. Most are Zoom oral arguments in single cases: the clerk announces 'The Court of Appeals for the Eighth District of Texas is now in session', the presiding justice calls the cause number, sets time limits and explains the timer, counsel argue with rebuttal, and the justices question them. Cases include civil appeals (oil and gas, energy, public-information requests, deeds and property, personal injury, environmental permits), criminal appeals, and original proceedings such as mandamus. Two recordings are swearing-in ceremonies at which a justice gives the attorney's oath to new lawyers. One is a contempt / order-to-show-cause hearing in two criminal appeals, and one is an evidentiary hearing in a judicial-conduct matter in which the justices sit as a court of review.
participants: The Chief Justice and justices of the court; the court clerk; appellate counsel for the parties, including assistant district attorneys for the State, attorneys for cities, counties and a state university, and private civil counsel; in the show-cause hearing, the respondent attorney; in the judicial-conduct hearing, counsel for the State Commission on Judicial Conduct and for the judge; and at swearing-in ceremonies, newly licensed attorneys, their families and members of the local bar.
decisions: Rulings are generally not announced at argument. Cases are taken 'under advisement' and decided later in written opinions. In the show-cause hearing the court says a written order setting the respondent's obligations will follow. The judicial-conduct hearing ends with post-hearing submissions to come. At the swearing-in ceremonies new attorneys take the oath.
notes: Arguments name private litigants and criminal defendants, and the show-cause hearing concerns a named attorney's conduct. Most uploads carry Zoom's default title 'My Meeting', so case and date information is sparse, and many dates are upload batch dates rather than hearing dates. The presiding role passes between justices over the period.

name: City of West Miami City Commission
description: Zoom recordings of City of West Miami, Florida, City Commission meetings from 2020-2021, first fully virtual and later hybrid, along with two Planning and Zoning Board hearings. The mayor presides over the vice mayor and commissioners, with the city clerk, city manager, city attorney and department directors reporting, and residents may comment remotely. The commission votes on resolutions, contracts, budget and relief-program items and board appointments, while the Planning and Zoning Board rules on property variance requests after sworn testimony.
meetings_about: Regular, special and emergency City Commission meetings (about 20-175 minutes), first fully virtual from April 2020 and hybrid from November 2020 under a commission resolution, plus two Planning and Zoning Board hearings. Commission meetings follow a set order: welcome by the mayor, the clerk reading Zoom/phone participation instructions, invocation, pledge, roll call, approval of minutes, public comments (three minutes each), city manager's report and numbered agenda items with motions and roll-call or voice votes.
participants: Mayor (presiding), vice mayor and commissioners; city clerk, city manager, city attorney, planning and zoning director, police chief and other staff; outside consultants/auditors; public commenters. Planning and Zoning hearings: board chair and members, city attorney, planning and zoning director, applicants and neighbouring residents, who are sworn in.
decisions: The commission adopts resolutions (including one authorising hybrid meetings), approves minutes, awards bids and contracts (e.g. water-line projects), allocates CARES Act-funded programs and utility credits, handles budget matters and board appointments, and swears in elected officials. The Planning and Zoning Board hears and votes on variance requests for residential construction.
notes: Later meetings are hybrid, with an in-room camera tile carrying several speakers (e.g. tiles named 'Mlami Commi'/'Commi'). Zoom meeting IDs and phone numbers are read aloud; applicants and neighbours give home addresses in zoning hearings.

name: Hunter's Hill Council
region: Hunters Hill, New South Wales, Australia
description: Recordings of Hunter's Hill Council meetings (a local government area in Sydney, New South Wales) held from 2020 to 2022, mainly ordinary council meetings plus extraordinary meetings and sessions of the Local Planning Panel. The Mayor chairs debates in which councillors move, second and vote on staff reports and motions, and council staff answer questions. Council decides on policies, plans, finances and appointments such as the election of the Mayor. The Local Planning Panel hears applicants and residents and determines development applications.
meetings_about: 23 recordings from April 2020 to April 2022. Most are ordinary council meetings, identified by sequential meeting number (e.g. 4477-4506) and often split into several parts. There are also two extraordinary meetings, one of which elects the Mayor and Deputy Mayor, and two sessions of the Hunter's Hill Local Planning Panel. Council meetings open with an acknowledgement of country, then confirmation of minutes, mayoral minutes and notices of motion, then staff reports taken item by item on a mover and seconder, with debate and 'all those in favour / against' votes. Councillors put questions 'through the Mayor' to the General Manager and directors. Confidential items are dealt with off-air. Planning Panel sessions have an independent chair, expert members and a community representative. They hear applicants and objectors on development applications, with three minutes per speaker.
participants: The Mayor (chair), the Deputy Mayor and councillors; the General Manager and directors (e.g. finance and corporate strategy, development); members of the community who register to address council. At Planning Panel sessions: the panel chair (a solicitor), expert members (town planner, heritage consultant), a community representative, council planning staff, applicants and their consultants, and neighbours or objectors.
decisions: Council adopts or amends staff recommendations and councillors' motions: policies and plans (e.g. a flood-study approach and a park plan of management, a drone policy), investment reports, fees and waivers, committee minutes and delegations. It also elects the Mayor and Deputy Mayor at an extraordinary meeting. The Local Planning Panel determines development applications for alterations and new dwellings in heritage areas, or defers them. At least one panel decision is said to be 'available later' and is not announced during the recording.
notes: Meetings are split across multiple uploads, and the collection holds only some parts of some meetings. Speaker attribution is unreliable in places: panel members' speech is attributed to other tiles, and labels such as 'WORDS' and variant spellings of councillors' names appear. Members of the public, including applicants and neighbours, speak at Planning Panel hearings about named private properties. The mayoralty changes during the period, so the same person appears under both 'Mayor' and 'Clr' labels.

name: Town of Kensington Town Council
description: Monthly Town Council meetings of the Town of Kensington, Maryland, held on Zoom between August 2021 and December 2022 and posted in gallery view by the county's municipal cable channel. The mayor, council members and the town manager conduct town business and hear from residents during public appearances and from invited presenters. The council adopts resolutions on contracts, traffic and parking, appointments and capital projects, holds public hearings, and passes ordinances, including the annual budget and a charter amendment.
sensitivity: Street addresses are read out.
meetings_about: Sixteen monthly regular Town Council meetings on Zoom from August 2021 to December 2022, posted in gallery view by the county's municipal cable channel, each running roughly 50 minutes to 3 hours. The mayor calls the meeting to order and a moment of silence follows. The agenda then covers approval of minutes, mayor and council reports, the town manager's report, public appearances by residents, invited presentations, and ordinances, resolutions and regulations, with public hearings held on ordinances and charter resolutions. Votes are by voice ('all those in favor').
participants: The mayor, town council members, the town manager, the town attorney, invited presenters (e.g. county officials, developers and working groups), and residents speaking during public appearances or asking questions on items.
decisions: Resolutions authorizing the town manager to contract for work such as speed humps and bridge and stormwater studies, and to set street parking restrictions; confirming mayoral appointments to town boards; amending the capital improvement plan. Ordinances, including adoption of the fiscal year 2022-23 budget. A charter resolution and matching ordinance on council qualifications and elections. Approval of minutes and grants. The council comments on county-controlled development and planning matters but does not decide them.
notes: Published by a third-party public-access channel, not the town. One upload's title (July 11, 2022) does not match its listed date. Street addresses and names of residents are read out. Moments of silence mention private individuals' deaths and family events.

name: Town of Pittsfield Town Council and committees
description: Zoom recordings from the Town of Pittsfield, Maine, dated 2021, mostly regular Town Council meetings, along with Planning Board, Finance, Ordinance, Airport and Parks and Recreation committee meetings. The mayor chairs the council, and the town manager, councillors, committee members, applicants and residents take part. The council adopts ordinances, resolutions and spending orders and sets public hearings, while the boards and committees review land-use applications and prepare budgets, programs and ordinance drafts.
meetings_about: Regular Town Council meetings (some with a preceding workshop), 70-240 minutes, plus single meetings of the Planning Board (including a board training on subdivision regulations), Parks and Recreation, Finance, Airport and Ordinance committees, February-October 2021. Council meetings are chaired by the mayor and follow an agenda of public hearings, committee reports, town manager's report, old and new business with motions and votes, and councillor comments.
participants: Mayor (council chair), deputy mayor and town councillors; the town manager, who hosts the Zoom sessions and reports; town staff; committee and board members and chairs; applicants before the Planning Board; residents who comment.
decisions: The council enacts and sets public hearings on ordinances (e.g. a revised general assistance ordinance, a proposed consumer fireworks ordinance), passes resolutions and orders (e.g. purchases such as winter sand, a road-paving petition), and reviews budgets and committee recommendations. The Planning Board reviews site applications (e.g. a town waterfront/canoe-access project); committees prepare budgets, programs and ordinance drafts for the council.
notes: Mixes the governing council with several advisory committees and the Planning Board. About 8% of words carry no speaker name; some pre-meeting small talk is recorded. One recording lacks a date.

name: Madison Heights City Council
region: Madison Heights, Oakland County, Michigan, USA
description: Recordings of remote Madison Heights, Michigan City Council meetings from April 2020 to June 2021. Participants are the mayor, council members, the city manager, city clerk and other staff, and residents speaking during public comment and public hearings. The council votes by roll call on ordinances, including zoning amendments, resolutions, bid awards and purchases, and budget matters.
meetings_about: Regular (and occasional special) City Council meetings held remotely in 2020-2021, typically starting at 7:30 pm. The mayor calls the meeting to order, the clerk takes roll with each member stating their remote location, then council hears public comment and works through the agenda: public hearings, city manager reports on each item, motions, support (seconds) and roll-call votes, unfinished and new business, and council comments. Meetings run about 50 minutes to 3 hours; by June 2021 the chair sat in chambers while others joined remotely.
participants: The mayor and mayor pro tem, council members, the city manager, city clerk, city attorney and other department staff, county representatives on occasion, and residents speaking during public comment and public hearings.
decisions: Council adopts ordinances on first and second reading (including zoning amendments on building heights and adult-use marijuana establishments, animal-control changes), passes resolutions (e.g. emergency polling-location changes, poverty tax exemption guidelines), awards bids and approves purchases and contracts, schedules and holds public hearings (e.g. brownfield plans), works on the city budget, and makes board appointments.
notes: About 11% of words carry no speaker name, and shared room, host or role tiles carry about 9% of attributed words; some members' tiles are misspelled or change names across meetings. A few phone numbers are read aloud.

name: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
description: Recordings of remote oral arguments before three-judge panels of the District of Columbia Court of Appeals, the highest court of the District of Columbia. In each session a clerk opens court, the presiding judge calls cases from the calendar, and counsel for appellants and appellees argue while the judges question them about criminal, family, administrative and civil appeals. Cases are taken under advisement at the end of argument, and decisions are issued later in writing, not in these recordings.
sensitivity: Arguments name private litigants.
meetings_about: Ten remote (Zoom) oral argument sessions, each about 1.5-2.75 hours. A clerk's cry opens each session ('This Honorable Court is now in session'). The presiding judge welcomes participants to the virtual sitting and calls two or three cases from the day's calendar by docket number. In each case appellant's counsel argues first and may reserve rebuttal time, the appellee answers, and the three-judge panel questions counsel throughout. The panel is sometimes reconstituted between cases. Cases include criminal appeals (Fourth Amendment suppression, jury instructions, cell-site evidence), family-court child support, agency and employment matters, zoning (BZA) and civil contract or tort disputes. Recording dates are not in the metadata.
participants: Panels of three judges, including the Chief Judge, associate judges and a judge sitting by designation from D.C. Superior Court; the courtroom clerk; appellate counsel for the parties, such as the United States Attorney's Office, defense counsel and private civil counsel; and occasionally self-represented parties.
decisions: No rulings are announced at argument. At the end of each argument the presiding judge says the case is 'submitted' or 'taken under advisement', and the court decides later in written opinions. The recordings contain the judges' questions and counsel's arguments, not the decisions.
notes: Arguments name private litigants and discuss criminal cases, a child-support dispute involving minor children, and workplace injury and PTSD claims. Meeting dates and titles are missing, and one source file has a malformed video id ('CQKG9RtypFU&t'). Speaker labels are Zoom usernames (for example 'judgeglickman', 'courtroomclerk'), and some are mismatched, such as a counsel tile labelled with another name.

name: Town of Pine Plains Town Board
region: Pine Plains, Dutchess County, New York, USA
description: Zoom meetings of the Town Board of Pine Plains, a town in Dutchess County, New York, held from 2020 onward, including regular monthly meetings, workshop meetings and a public hearing on zoning map changes. The town supervisor and board members conduct business with the town clerk, attorney, engineer, planning consultants and residents. The board votes on minutes, bills, contracts and resolutions, adopts the budget and a police reform plan, and considers local laws revising the town's zoning.
sensitivity: The attorney--client session may contain privileged discussion posted publicly.
meetings_about: Fourteen Zoom meetings streamed live to YouTube, running about 1 to 2 hours. They are monthly regular Town Board meetings and workshop meetings, plus one session including an attorney-client portion and one public hearing on zoning map changes. Most titles carry no date; transcripts mention dates from May 2020 into 2021, e.g. a January 21, 2021 meeting. Regular meetings follow a set order: call to order, approval of minutes and the town clerk's report, approval of bills (general, highway, water district), the supervisor's statement, public comment, guest presentations, attorney and engineer reports, resolutions, and a motion to adjourn, sometimes into executive session. Workshops are more conversational.
participants: The town supervisor and town board members, the town clerk, the town attorney, the town engineer, planning consultants presenting the zoning review, invited guests (e.g. a USDA wildlife official), and residents giving public comment.
decisions: Approval of minutes, clerk's reports and payment of bills; resolutions authorizing contracts (e.g. USDA nuisance-goose control, zoning code revision consultants); records-retention and delegate resolutions; the town budget; a police reform and modernization plan required by the state; and local laws amending zoning, preceded by public hearings on zoning text and map changes.
notes: Most titles lack dates, and exact meeting dates are only partly recoverable from the recordings. One upload is titled as an attorney-client session and may include privileged discussion. Meetings include informal pre-meeting conversation before the call to order. Transcription is incomplete (15 of 17 listed meetings).

name: Fifth District Court of Appeals of Texas (Dallas)
description: Zoom recordings of oral arguments before three-justice panels of the Fifth District Court of Appeals of Texas in Dallas, dated 2020. Each recording covers one civil or criminal appeal, in which attorneys for the appellant and appellee (including prosecutors for the State in criminal cases) argue within timed limits while the justices question them. No decision is announced at argument: each case is declared submitted, and a written opinion follows later.
sensitivity: Captions name private litigants; at least one family-law appeal is captioned with the parties' initials, the convention Texas uses to protect children.
meetings_about: Zoom oral arguments in 2020 (mostly October-November), each recording a single case titled with its docket number (05-xx-xxxxx-CV or -CR) and caption, typically 20-75 minutes. A clerk opens with 'the Fifth District Court of Appeals in Dallas, Texas is now in session, Justice ... presiding'; the presiding justice calls the case and sets time (typically 20 minutes per side plus 5 for appellant's rebuttal) and the panel questions counsel. Cases include criminal appeals and civil appeals (commercial, tort, probate/trust, and family matters involving children).
participants: Three-justice panels with a presiding justice; court clerk staff opening the session; appellant and appellee attorneys, including appellate defense counsel and assistant district attorneys for the State of Texas in criminal cases.
decisions: No rulings are announced at argument. The presiding justice declares the case submitted and says an opinion will issue in due course.
notes: Case captions in titles name private litigants; family-law appeals involving children are captioned by initials. Arguments discuss criminal facts and abuse allegations in some cases.

name: Seventh Court of Appeals of Texas
description: Recordings of Zoom oral arguments before the Seventh Court of Appeals of Texas in Amarillo, held from 2020 to 2022, in civil and criminal appeals, plus two conferences of Special Courts of Review in judicial-conduct matters. Participants are the court's justices, the court clerk, and attorneys for appellants, appellees and the State. Attorneys argue their cases and answer the justices' questions; no decisions are announced in the recordings, as cases are taken under submission for later written opinions.
sensitivity: Case captions name private litigants.
meetings_about: Zoom oral arguments before three-justice panels in civil and criminal appeals, one case per recording (about 25 to 65 minutes), opened by the court clerk ('The Honorable Court of Appeals for the 7th District of Texas is now in session'). The presiding chief justice calls the case, sets time (for example 20 minutes per side plus rebuttal), and counsel for appellant and appellee argue while the justices question them; the case is then declared submitted. Two recordings are pretrial/pre-hearing conferences of Special Courts of Review, panels of appellate justices appointed by the Texas Supreme Court to review State Commission on Judicial Conduct sanctions of judges, presided over by this court's chief justice.
participants: The chief justice and justices of the court (and justices of other courts of appeals on special courts of review); the court clerk; attorneys for appellants and appellees, including prosecutors for the State in criminal appeals; counsel for the State Commission on Judicial Conduct and for respondent judges.
decisions: No rulings are announced at argument: each case is taken under submission and decided later in written opinions not included in the recordings. Appeals cover civil matters (contracts, oil and gas, anti-SLAPP/TCPA motions, premises liability, trusts, unemployment tax, municipal disputes) and criminal convictions, plus one juvenile case. The special-court-of-review conferences set schedules, hearing format and discovery for judicial-discipline reviews.
notes: Case captions in titles name private litigants, and one appeal involves a child (identified by initials). Metadata dates are mostly an upload date (2022-02-03); spoken dates show arguments held between 2020 and 2022 (e.g. the October 7, 2020 settings). Some appeals appear to originate outside the Panhandle (e.g. City of Buda, New Braunfels ISD), not otherwise explained in the recordings. Seven uploads without a gallery view are excluded.

name: Town of Westfield Town Council
description: Recordings of Town of Westfield, New Jersey, Town Council meetings held on Zoom from 2020 to 2022, including regular meetings, conference sessions and an annual reorganization meeting. The mayor chairs, council members present committee business, town staff report, and residents give public comment through Zoom. The council votes by roll call on resolutions and ordinances covering contracts, budget transfers, tax abatements and redevelopment, and it adopts the annual municipal budget.
meetings_about: 18 meetings from May 2020 to January 2022, streamed live on Facebook with public participation only through Zoom. The set includes regular Town Council meetings, conference sessions and the January 2021 reorganization meeting. Most run 30-110 minutes, and one runs about 3.5 hours. The mayor reads the Open Public Meetings Act notice and the clerk calls the roll, followed by reports (mayor's COVID-19 and town updates, town administrator, committee chairs), public comment, and committee chairs moving resolutions and ordinances on first or second reading, with roll-call votes. Conference sessions preview resolutions and hear presentations, such as a downtown redevelopment plan.
participants: The mayor (who chairs), council members, the town clerk, the town administrator, the town attorney and other staff such as the CFO and redevelopment counsel or planners, and residents who comment through Zoom.
decisions: The council adopts resolutions (contract awards such as the pool concession, CFO warrants and refunds, budget transfers, payments such as police body-worn cameras) and ordinances on first and second reading (e.g. property maintenance code amendments, a five-year tax exemption and abatement ordinance, downtown tax incentives). It introduces and adopts the municipal budget after a public hearing, acts on redevelopment plans, and makes annual appointments at reorganization.
notes: About 22% of words carry no speaker name, and labels are often truncated or garbled forms of council members' names (e.g. 'Mark', 'Lind', 'ounciwoman Uind'). The clerk's roll calls are sometimes attributed to the wrong tile. Meetings include COVID-19 case updates that mention deaths without naming anyone. The earlier notes mention a mayoral talk on public spaces, but the released titles all name council meetings.

name: District of Lantzville Council
description: Zoom recordings of regular and special meetings of the District of Lantzville Council, a small municipality on Vancouver Island, British Columbia. The mayor chairs a five-member council, with the chief administrative officer and district staff presenting reports, and delegations, applicants and registered members of the public addressing council. Council gives readings to and adopts bylaws such as the tax rates and financial plan bylaws, issues development and variance permits, receives the annual audit, and directs staff through motions.
meetings_about: Nine Zoom-streamed council meetings from May 2021 to May 2022: seven regular council meetings (about 1.5-2.5 hours, starting at 6 p.m.) and two special meetings (one about 2 hours, one 15 minutes for an audit presentation). The mayor calls the meeting to order, gives a territorial acknowledgement of the Snuneymuxw First Nation, and moves adoption of the agenda; the meeting then proceeds through public input from registered speakers (two minutes each), delegations and presentations, staff reports, bylaws, and council motions with mover/seconder debate conducted 'through the chair'.
participants: The mayor (chair) and four councillors, the chief administrative officer and district directors/staff, invited delegations (e.g. external auditors, consultants), development applicants, and members of the public registered to speak.
decisions: Council gives bylaws first, second and third readings and adoption (e.g. annual tax rates bylaw, five-year financial plan and amendments), issues development permits and development variance permits, receives the audited financial statements, directs staff on reports (e.g. development impact assessments, beach and park improvements, streetscape budget), and adopts agendas and minutes.
notes: Small collection (9 meetings, about 17.5 hours). About 15% of words have no speaker name and 10% are attributed to shared room or host tiles; speaker labels contain OCR noise in councillor names. Public speakers state their names and addresses on the record.

name: Town of Pompey Town Board and boards
region: Pompey, Onondaga County, New York, USA
description: Recordings of virtual meetings of Town of Pompey, New York bodies from 2020 to 2022: the Town Board, Zoning Board of Appeals, Planning Board and Environmental Conservation Commission. Participants are the town supervisor and council members, board and commission members, town staff such as the clerk, attorney and code officer, applicants, and residents. The Town Board adopts the town budget and considers local laws such as a solar energy overlay district, while the Zoning Board of Appeals decides variance applications and the Planning Board reviews subdivisions and environmental determinations.
sensitivity: Applicants speak in Zoning Board of Appeals hearings.
meetings_about: Virtual meetings (streamed on Zoom and Facebook under the governor's pandemic executive order) of several Town of Pompey bodies, 2020-2022: monthly and special Town Board meetings, Zoning Board of Appeals public meetings, a Planning Board meeting with public hearing, and Environmental Conservation Commission meetings (including its organizational meeting). Town Board meetings open with the Pledge of Allegiance and introductions, then public hearings, reports, and motions voted by voice ('all those in favor ... motion carried'). Recordings run about 20 minutes to 2.5 hours.
participants: The town supervisor and town council members; the town clerk, town attorney, accountant, highway superintendent, code enforcement officer and web/Zoom manager; Zoning Board of Appeals and Planning Board chairs and members; Environmental Conservation Commission volunteers; applicants and developers (e.g. a community solar company); and residents commenting at public hearings.
decisions: The Town Board adopts the annual town budget after a public hearing, considers local laws (including a solar energy systems overlay district law and a special events law), approves budget transfers, contracts and intermunicipal agreements, and approves minutes. The Zoning Board of Appeals grants or denies area variances, sometimes with conditions tied to subdivision approval; the Planning Board makes SEQR determinations and reviews subdivisions and site plans. The Environmental Conservation Commission discusses and advises but does not make binding decisions.
notes: Pools several town bodies. Applicants and residents speak about their own properties in variance and planning hearings. The web/Zoom manager's tile appears to carry speech by others in some meetings, so attribution to that tile is unreliable.

name: Tecumseh Public Schools Board of Education
description: Zoom recordings of Tecumseh Public Schools Board of Education meetings in Michigan, dated 2020-2021, including regular and special meetings and budget sessions. The board president runs the meetings with trustees, the superintendent and district finance staff, and there is a public comment period. The board votes on budgets and budget revisions, purchases, fee schedules, contract extensions, policies and board officer elections, and discusses COVID-era school operations.
sensitivity: School boards may seat student representatives, who may be minors.
meetings_about: Regular and special Board of Education meetings, a budget workshop and a combined budget hearing and regular meeting, April 2020 to February 2021 (17-156 minutes). Meetings are livestreamed by district technology staff and follow a standard agenda: call to order, pledge, public comment (often no registrants), agenda approval, 'good news' items, financial reports, discussion and action items, superintendent's report and closing; the January 2021 organisational meeting elects board officers.
participants: Board president (chair), vice president and trustees; the superintendent; district finance/business services staff; technology staff running the livestream; occasional other administrators. Public participation is evident only as a public-comment agenda slot, usually with no registrants.
decisions: The board approves agendas, budgets and final budget revisions, CARES Act-funded purchases (e.g. Chromebooks), facility use fee schedules, contract extensions (e.g. food service), board policies and superintendent goals, considers resolutions such as emergency powers for the superintendent, and elects its officers. It also debates school reconfiguration, busing contracts and COVID-era instruction plans.
notes: Meeting dates appear only in titles, in a space-separated form (e.g. '5 11 2020'). Some tiles are device- or household-named. No student representatives are evident in the recordings.

name: City of Reynoldsburg council and commissions
description: Recordings of public meetings of the City of Reynoldsburg, Ohio, from 2020 to 2021, covering City Council, the Planning Commission, the Community Commission and the organizational meeting of the Civilian Review Board, plus two episodes of a talk show hosted by the mayor. Participants include the mayor, council members, the clerk, city staff and attorney, appointed commission and board members, and residents giving public comment. Council adopts ordinances, resolutions and proclamations, and the Planning Commission reviews site plans for development. The Community Commission coordinates volunteer committees and does not make binding decisions.
meetings_about: Nine recordings from August 2020 to September 2021, streamed live on Facebook.
